questions.question: Explain the process of catagenesis and its important in hydrocarbon generation.
questions.solution_html:
• • Catagenesis is the intermediate stage in the transformation of buried organic matter, where
  • increasing heat and pressure (about 60–120°C) break down kerogen through thermal cracking.
  • This temperature range is called the oil window, where kerogen decomposes into liquid
  • hydrocarbons (oil) and gaseous hydrocarbons (natural gas). ((1.5 marks))
  • • It is highly significant because different types of kerogen generate varying amounts of oil
  • and gas, and the efficiency of catagenesis determines how much hydrocarbon a source rock
  • can produce. The process also influences the physical and chemical properties of the
  • hydrocarbons, affecting their migration and accumulation in reservoir rocks. Thus
  • catagenesis is a key stage directly linked to economic hydrocarbon generation. ((1.5 marks))
questions.final_answer: Option (c) break down kerogen through thermal cracking.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: Describe the transition of oil window to gas window.
questions.solution_html:
• The transition from oil window to gas window occurs as the subsurface temperatures rise beyond
  • 120°C. In the oil window (60–120°C), kerogen mainly breaks down to form liquid hydrocarbons.
  • When temperatures exceed 120°C, the process enters the gas window (about 120–200°C), where
  • remaining kerogen and previously formed oil undergo further thermal cracking to produce natural
  • gas, mainly methane. At even higher temperatures, the capacity for hydrocarbon generation
  • declines, and organic matter may decompose into non-hydrocarbon residues. This transition
  • marks the shift from oil formation to dominant gas production during burial and heating. (Any 3
  • Points – (3 marks))
questions.final_answer: Option (c) In the oil window (60–120°C), kerogen mainly breaks down to form liquid hydrocarbons.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: Question 13

• Compile electromagnetic methods with seismic surveys in oil exploration techniques.
  • Electromagnetic (EM) methods and seismic surveys are complementary geophysical techniques
  • used in petroleum exploration. EM methods investigate subsurface electrical conductivity

  • waves, geophysicists can locate traps, faults, folds, and other structural features. Together, EM
  • and seismic methods improve accuracy in identifying potential hydrocarbon reservoirs. (Any 3

questions.question: Explain the differences between proved, probable, and possible reserves in petroleum
questions.solution_html:
• exploration.
  • (Any 2 points each for proved, probable, and possible reserves Give Full credit)
  • Proved, probable, and possible reserves represent different levels of confidence in the
  • recoverability of petroleum resources and are essential for evaluating the economic potential of
  • an oil or gas field. Proved reserves are the most reliable estimates. They refer to quantities of
  • petroleum that can be recovered with reasonable certainty from known reservoirs under current
  • economic conditions, operating methods, and government regulations. In deterministic methods
  • this means a high degree of confidence, while in probabilistic terms, there is at least a 90%
  • probability of recovery. Proved reserves are further subdivided into developed (ready for
  • production) and undeveloped (requiring additional drilling or infrastructure).
  • Probable reserves fall under unproved reserves but have a higher likelihood of being recovered
  • compared to possible reserves. They rely on geological and engineering data but lack the certainty
  • of proved reserves due to technical or economic uncertainties. Probable reserves are considered
  • more likely than not to be recoverable, typically with at least a 50% probability. However, they
  • may not be extracted if economic conditions make recovery unfeasible.
  • Possible reserves represent the least certain category among the three. They are also unproved
  • reserves but have a lower chance of successful extraction compared to probable reserves.
  • Geological and engineering data indicate that they are less likely to be recovered, with a
  • probability of at least 10%. These reserves often depend on future technological improvements
  • or changes in economic conditions to become viable.
  • The key difference lies in the degree of confidence: proved reserves offer the highest certainty of
  • commercial recovery, probable reserves indicate moderate confidence, and possible reserves
  • reflect low confidence, making them the most uncertain category in petroleum exploration.
questions.final_answer: reflect low confidence, making them the most uncertain category in petroleum exploration

questions.question: Question 19
questions.solution_html:
• Compare the electrical and resistivity methods in subsurface exploration. How do these
  • techniques work, and in what contexts are they most effective?
  • (Explanation on electrical and resistivity method (5 marks) and answer to most effectiveness of the
  • method (2 marks))
  • The electrical method measures the general electrical resistivity of subsurface rocks.
  • Hydrocarbons are poor conductors, so formations containing oil or gas show higher resistivity
  • compared to water-saturated rocks. This method uses electrodes placed on the surface or in
  • boreholes to pass current and measure potential differences. It helps map subsurface structures
  • and locate possible reservoirs. The method is simple, low-cost, and useful in areas where seismic
  • surveys are difficult, though it has a limited depth of investigation and can be influenced by soil
  • moisture, clay content, and surface conductivity.
  • The resistivity method, a more specific technique within electrical surveys, focuses on measuring
  • the electrical resistance of rocks to identify hydrocarbon zones. Since hydrocarbons increase
  • resistivity, this method is widely used in well logging and surface surveys to distinguish between
  • hydrocarbon-bearing and water-bearing formations. It also helps estimate formation thickness
  • and porosity. Although it is non-invasive and effective, its accuracy can be affected by the salinity
  • of formation water and clay content, and it requires careful calibration, especially in
  • heterogeneous formations.
  • Overall, electrical methods are most effective for broad subsurface mapping and identifying
  • resistivity contrasts near the surface, while resistivity methods are particularly valuable in well
  • logging and detailed reservoir characterization. Together, they provide essential information for
  • identifying and evaluating potential hydrocarbon reservoirs.
questions.final_answer: identifying and evaluating potential hydrocarbon reservoirs
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: Question 20
questions.solution_html:
• Relate geobotanical techniques with other surface exploration methods like geochemical or
  • geological exploration.
  • (Give (2.5 marks) each for three points of geobotanical and geochemical method and for geological
  • exploration give (2 marks))
  • Geobotanical exploration is an important surface exploration technique that complements other
  • methods such as geochemical and geological exploration in petroleum prospecting. Geobotanical
  • methods rely on studying vegetation type, distribution, and health to detect anomalies caused by
  • natural hydrocarbon seepages. Certain plants absorb trace hydrocarbons or show stress when
  • exposed to altered soil chemistry, making them useful indicators of subsurface petroleum. Like
  • geochemical exploration, geobotanical techniques are non-invasive, cost-effective, and useful for
  • early-stage identification of prospective zones. Both methods provide indirect evidence of
  • hydrocarbons and help narrow down targets before expensive drilling or geophysical surveys.
  • Geochemical methods analyze soils, rocks, gases, and water for hydrocarbon microseepages
  • while geobotanical methods focus on plant responses. Both techniques may be affected by
  • environmental factors, leading to false positives or negatives, highlighting the need for integration
  • with other surveys. Compared to geological exploration, which examines rock types, structural
  • features, folds, faults, and sedimentary basins, geobotanical surveys offer an advantage in
  • vegetation-covered or remote regions where rock exposures are limited. Geological methods
  • provide essential information about basin structure but are restricted to surface features and may
  • not reveal deeper reservoirs. Geobotanical indicators help refine geological interpretations by
  • pointing to potential seepage zones.
questions.final_answer: pointing to potential seepage zones

questions.question: Explain the impact of olefins on the refining process of crude oil.
questions.solution_html:
• (Any 5 points give (7 marks))
  • Olefins are unsaturated hydrocarbons, which means the double bond is present between the two
  • carbon atoms in the formula. The generic formula is (C H ), and the lowest member of this
  • n 2n
  • homologous series is ethylene, C H .This series is known as alkenes. These are highly reactive
  • 2 4
  • and can react to themselves to mono olefins. Olefins are not present in crude oil, but they are
  • produced by thermal and catalytic decomposition or dehydrogenation of normal paraffins. Olefins
  • can complicate the refining process because their double bonds make them more reactive, which
  • can lead to polymerization or other unwanted reactions. They are often targeted for conversion
  • into more stable compounds during refining. Olefins are generally undesirable in finished products

questions.question: Explain the process of catagenesis and its important in hydrocarbon generation.
questions.solution_html:

  • hydrocarbons (oil) and gaseous hydrocarbons (natural gas). ((1.5 marks))

  • and gas, and the efficiency of catagenesis determines how much hydrocarbon a source rock
  • can produce. The process also influences the physical and chemical properties of the
  • hydrocarbons, affecting their migration and accumulation in reservoir rocks. Thus
  • catagenesis is a key stage directly linked to economic hydrocarbon generation. ((1.5 marks))

questions.question: Describe the transition of oil window to gas window.
questions.solution_html:
• The transition from oil window to gas window occurs as the subsurface temperatures rise beyond
  • 120°C. In the oil window (60–120°C), kerogen mainly breaks down to form liquid hydrocarbons.
  • When temperatures exceed 120°C, the process enters the gas window (about 120–200°C), where
  • remaining kerogen and previously formed oil undergo further thermal cracking to produce natural
  • gas, mainly methane. At even higher temperatures, the capacity for hydrocarbon generation
  • declines, and organic matter may decompose into non-hydrocarbon residues. This transition
  • marks the shift from oil formation to dominant gas production during burial and heating. (Any 3
  • Points – (3 marks))

questions.question: Explain the differences between proved, probable, and possible reserves in petroleum
questions.solution_html:
• exploration.
  • (Any 2 points each for proved, probable, and possible reserves Give Full credit)
  • Proved, probable, and possible reserves represent different levels of confidence in the
  • recoverability of petroleum resources and are essential for evaluating the economic potential of
  • an oil or gas field. Proved reserves are the most reliable estimates. They refer to quantities of
  • petroleum that can be recovered with reasonable certainty from known reservoirs under current
  • economic conditions, operating methods, and government regulations. In deterministic methods
  • this means a high degree of confidence, while in probabilistic terms, there is at least a 90%
  • probability of recovery. Proved reserves are further subdivided into developed (ready for
  • production) and undeveloped (requiring additional drilling or infrastructure).
  • Probable reserves fall under unproved reserves but have a higher likelihood of being recovered
  • compared to possible reserves. They rely on geological and engineering data but lack the certainty
  • of proved reserves due to technical or economic uncertainties. Probable reserves are considered
  • more likely than not to be recoverable, typically with at least a 50% probability. However, they
  • may not be extracted if economic conditions make recovery unfeasible.
  • Possible reserves represent the least certain category among the three. They are also unproved
  • reserves but have a lower chance of successful extraction compared to probable reserves.
  • Geological and engineering data indicate that they are less likely to be recovered, with a
  • probability of at least 10%. These reserves often depend on future technological improvements
  • or changes in economic conditions to become viable.
  • The key difference lies in the degree of confidence: proved reserves offer the highest certainty of
  • commercial recovery, probable reserves indicate moderate confidence, and possible reserves
  • reflect low confidence, making them the most uncertain category in petroleum exploration.
questions.final_answer: reflect low confidence, making them the most uncertain category in petroleum exploration

questions.question: Question 19
questions.solution_html:
• Compare the electrical and resistivity methods in subsurface exploration. How do these
  • techniques work, and in what contexts are they most effective?
  • (Explanation on electrical and resistivity method (5 marks) and answer to most effectiveness of the
  • method (2 marks))
  • The electrical method measures the general electrical resistivity of subsurface rocks.
  • Hydrocarbons are poor conductors, so formations containing oil or gas show higher resistivity
  • compared to water-saturated rocks. This method uses electrodes placed on the surface or in
  • boreholes to pass current and measure potential differences. It helps map subsurface structures
  • and locate possible reservoirs. The method is simple, low-cost, and useful in areas where seismic
  • surveys are difficult, though it has a limited depth of investigation and can be influenced by soil
  • moisture, clay content, and surface conductivity.
  • The resistivity method, a more specific technique within electrical surveys, focuses on measuring
  • the electrical resistance of rocks to identify hydrocarbon zones. Since hydrocarbons increase
  • resistivity, this method is widely used in well logging and surface surveys to distinguish between
  • hydrocarbon-bearing and water-bearing formations. It also helps estimate formation thickness
  • and porosity. Although it is non-invasive and effective, its accuracy can be affected by the salinity
  • of formation water and clay content, and it requires careful calibration, especially in
  • heterogeneous formations.
  • Overall, electrical methods are most effective for broad subsurface mapping and identifying
  • resistivity contrasts near the surface, while resistivity methods are particularly valuable in well
  • logging and detailed reservoir characterization. Together, they provide essential information for
  • identifying and evaluating potential hydrocarbon reservoirs.
questions.final_answer: identifying and evaluating potential hydrocarbon reservoirs

questions.question: Question 20

  • exploration give (2 marks))
  • Geobotanical exploration is an important surface exploration technique that complements other
  • methods such as geochemical and geological exploration in petroleum prospecting. Geobotanical
  • methods rely on studying vegetation type, distribution, and health to detect anomalies caused by
  • natural hydrocarbon seepages. Certain plants absorb trace hydrocarbons or show stress when
  • exposed to altered soil chemistry, making them useful indicators of subsurface petroleum. Like
  • geochemical exploration, geobotanical techniques are non-invasive, cost-effective, and useful for
  • early-stage identification of prospective zones. Both methods provide indirect evidence of
  • hydrocarbons and help narrow down targets before expensive drilling or geophysical surveys.
  • Geochemical methods analyze soils, rocks, gases, and water for hydrocarbon microseepages
  • while geobotanical methods focus on plant responses. Both techniques may be affected by
  • environmental factors, leading to false positives or negatives, highlighting the need for integration
  • with other surveys. Compared to geological exploration, which examines rock types, structural
  • features, folds, faults, and sedimentary basins, geobotanical surveys offer an advantage in
  • vegetation-covered or remote regions where rock exposures are limited. Geological methods
  • provide essential information about basin structure but are restricted to surface features and may
  • not reveal deeper reservoirs. Geobotanical indicators help refine geological interpretations by
  • pointing to potential seepage zones.
questions.final_answer: pointing to potential seepage zones

questions.question: Explain the impact of olefins on the refining process of crude oil.
questions.solution_html:
• (Any 5 points give (7 marks))
  • Olefins are unsaturated hydrocarbons, which means the double bond is present between the two
  • carbon atoms in the formula. The generic formula is (C H ), and the lowest member of this
  • n 2n
  • homologous series is ethylene, C H .This series is known as alkenes. These are highly reactive
  • 2 4
  • and can react to themselves to mono olefins. Olefins are not present in crude oil, but they are
  • produced by thermal and catalytic decomposition or dehydrogenation of normal paraffins. Olefins
  • can complicate the refining process because their double bonds make them more reactive, which
  • can lead to polymerization or other unwanted reactions. They are often targeted for conversion
  • into more stable compounds during refining. Olefins are generally undesirable in finished products
  • because, the double bonds are reactive and the compounds are more easily oxidized and
  • polymerized to form gums and varnishes, so they can be removed by absorption in sulfuric
  • acid.The reactivity of olefins makes them valuable feedstocks in the petrochemical industry
  • particularly in the production of polymers, synthetic fibers, and chemicals.

questions.question: Discuss the significance of density in characterizing hydrocarbons and its implications for various
questions.solution_html:
• industries.
  • (Give (3 marks) for explanation on density characterization and (4 marks) to application)
  • Density is a fundamental physical property used to characterize hydrocarbons because it directly
  • reflects their composition, molecular structure, and behaviour under different conditions. Defined
  • as mass per unit volume, density changes significantly with temperature. As temperature
  • increases, molecular kinetic energy rises, causing hydrocarbons to expand and their density to
  • decrease. This temperature–density relationship is crucial for accurate measurement and handling
  • of petroleum products. In the oil and gas industry, understanding density is essential during
  • production, transportation, and refining. Pipelines must be designed to accommodate density
  • variations caused by temperature fluctuations to maintain smooth flow and prevent issues such as
  • phase separation or blockages. Density also influences reservoir evaluation, fluid modeling, and
  • metering systems used to calculate volumes and economic value.
  • In refining, density plays an important role in separation processes such as distillation, where
  • hydrocarbon fractions are separated based on boiling points related to molecular weight and
  • density. Accurate density measurement ensures product quality and helps classify fuels like
  • gasoline, diesel, and kerosene. Hydrometer method is commonly used for determining density.
  • Density has implications for transportation and storage logistics, influencing tank design, material
  • selection, and flow assurance. It is also relevant in environmental management, as density helps
  • predict how hydrocarbons behave during spills, including their spreading, mixing, and
  • biodegradation tendencies.
questions.final_answer: biodegradation tendencies
